rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion follows orphan abuse and failure to urge feeding: mistreatment wrongs creatures, while prayer without reverence is worse because it neglects service to the Creator.
rows.anchor: لأن الإيذاء والمنع من النفع معاملة مع المخلوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers the objection that prayer deters indecency: these worshipers’ prayer itself is made up of ostentation and heedlessness.
rows.anchor: الصلاة كيف تنهاه عن هذا الفعل المنكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neglecting compassion toward creation and reverence for God completes their wretchedness; “woe” marks a grave crime, as in three other warnings.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا اللفظ إنما يستعمل عند الجريمة الشديدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says each person in Hell wails according to his sin, including love of status, pre-Islamic zeal, or prayer; one should say, “Woe to me if God does not forgive me.”
rows.anchor: ويروى أن كل أحد ينوح في النار بحسب جريمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe threat concerns three acts—heedlessness about prayer, showing off, and withholding al-maʿūn—raising the question why sins that do not by themselves make one an unbeliever draw such punishment.
rows.anchor: الآية دالة على حصول التهديد العظيم بفعل ثلاثة أمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relied-upon answer reads “those who pray” as hypocrites who commit these acts, so the threat is directed at them.
rows.anchor: أي فويل للمصلين من المنافقين الذين يأتون بهذه الأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, unbelievers receive additional punishment for violating prohibitions and neglecting obligations, supporting al-Shāfiʿī’s view that they are addressed by the law’s subsidiary commands.
rows.anchor: وهو يدل على صحة قول الشافعي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s distinction: “heedless in their prayer” would threaten believers, whereas “heedless from their prayer” describes people who do not remember it and are detached from it.
rows.anchor: ما رواه عطاء عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī calls Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation weak: heedlessness from prayer cannot mean simply abandoning it, since the verse calls them worshipers, and such abandonment alone is neither hypocrisy nor unbelief.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول ضعيف لأن السهو عن الصلاة لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī answers that they count as worshipers outwardly but have forgotten prayer altogether inwardly, as hypocrites rise lazily, show off, and remember God only a little.
rows.anchor: حكم عليهم بكونهم مضلين نظرا إلى الصورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Complete failure to remember God in every part of prayer reflects a hypocrite’s belief that prayer is useless; a believer may instead become inattentive during some parts, so heedlessness “in” prayer differs from heedlessness “from” it.
rows.anchor: بل قد يحصل له السهو في الصلاة بمعنى أنه يصير ساهيا

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص ومسروق والحسن ومقاتل
rows.claim: Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Masrūq, al-Ḥasan, and Muqātil explain the phrase as failing to guard prayer times and conditions and not caring whether one prays.
rows.anchor: وهو قول سعد بن أبي وقاص ومسروق والحسن ومقاتل

rows.speaker: كثير من العلماء
rows.claim: Many scholars say the Prophet did not truly lapse in prayer; God enabled him to perform an act resembling a lapse so that he could demonstrate the law, whose practical demonstration is stronger.
rows.anchor: الله تعالى أذن له في ذلك الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One category is lapses by the Prophet and Companions, repaired either by the prostration of forgetfulness or by sunnah and voluntary prayers.
rows.anchor: سهو الرسول والصحابة وذلك منجبر تارة بسجود السهو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second category is distraction within prayer, including failure to summon one’s knowledge and intentions.
rows.anchor: ما يكون في الصلاة من الغفلة وعدم استحضار المعارف والنيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third category is leaving prayer without making it up and letting its time pass; a hypocrite’s token prayer is worse than leaving prayer because it mocks religion.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك صلاة المنافق وهي شر من ترك الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hypocrite displays faith while hiding unbelief; a show-off displays extra humility absent from his heart to appear devout. Alternatively, the hypocrite does not pray privately, while the show-off improves his prayer before people.
rows.anchor: أن المنافق هو المظهر للإيمان المبطن للكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obligatory prayer and almsgiving should be performed publicly as Islamic symbols; displaying them clears suspicion, since abandoning them merits a curse.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنه يجب إظهار الفرائض من الصلاة والزكاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Voluntary prayers are normally concealed, unless displaying them is intended to encourage imitation.
rows.anchor: إنما الإخفاء في النوافل إلا إذا أظهر النوافل ليقتدى به

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One person saw a man prolonging a prostration of gratitude in the mosque and remarked that it would have been admirable if done at home.
rows.anchor: وعن بعضهم أنه رأى في المسجد رجلا يسجد للشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The advice is neither to abandon voluntary prayers out of embarrassment nor to perform them for show; avoiding ostentation is rarely easy.
rows.anchor: لا يترك النوافل حياء ولا يأتي بها رياء

rows.speaker: النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام
rows.claim: The Prophet likens ostentation to something more hidden than a black ant crawling on a black surface in a dark night; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: الرياء أخفى من دبيب النملة السوداء في الليلة الظلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word murāʾāh is the reciprocal form of “showing”: the show-off displays his deed to people, who in turn offer praise and admiration.
rows.anchor: هي مفاعلة من الإراءة لأن المرائي يرى الناس عمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning about heedlessness covers missing prayer time and inattentiveness within prayer; this verse adds ostentation, so prayer should be free of all three faults.
rows.anchor: فظهر أن الصلاة يجب أن تكون خالية عن هذه الأحوال الثلاثة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر وعلي وابن عباس وابن الحنفية وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة والضحاك
rows.claim: Abū Bakr, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk identify al-maʿūn as zakāt.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي بكر وعلي وابن عباس وابن الحنفية

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from Ubayy says reciting Sūrat Araʾayta earns forgiveness if the reciter pays zakāt, which is taken to suggest al-maʿūn means zakāt.
rows.anchor: غفر الله له إن كان للزكاة مؤديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zakāt interpretation also fits the word’s placement immediately after prayer.
rows.anchor: ولأن الله تعالى ذكره عقيب الصلاة

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes say al-maʿūn is something ordinarily lent to rich or poor and not withheld without revealing vile manners, such as an axe, pot, bucket, fire striker, sieve, or adze.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني ) : وهو قول أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says three things may not lawfully be withheld: water, fire, and salt.
rows.anchor: فإنه روي : «ثلاثة لا يحل منعها

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: This customary lending includes letting a neighbor bake in one’s oven or leave belongings at one’s home for part of a day.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك أن يلتمس جارك أن يخبز في تنورك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this account, maʿūn derives from maʿn, a small thing; zakāt is a little taken from much, and familiar loaned utensils are likewise called maʿūn.
rows.anchor: قالوا : الماعون فاعول من المعن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading rebukes miserliness over small necessities as especially base; the hypocrites behaved this way, like those who hoard and urge others to hoard.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا التقدير يكون معنى الآية الزجر عن البخل

rows.speaker: العلماء
rows.claim: The scholars commend keeping more household necessities than one needs so neighbors can borrow them, rather than giving only what is obligatory.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء : ومن الفضائل أن يستكثر الرجل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports hearing an Arab use al-maʿūn for water and cites a line of poetry as evidence; the poet is not identified.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : سمعت بعض العرب يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Water is plausibly singled out because it is a costly absence and cheap plenty; water is also the first request of Hell’s inhabitants and an early delight of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وأول شيء يسأله أهل النار الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth explanation takes al-maʿūn as willing obedience, as in the expression about taming a camel until it gives obedience.
rows.anchor: القول الرابع ) : ( الماعون ) حسن الانقياد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers the broadest sense: every act of obedience that is easy to perform, because it yields more benefit.
rows.anchor: الأولى أن يحمل على كل طاعة يخف فعلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ostentatious prayer gives to people what belongs to God, while withholding al-maʿūn hides from people what is theirs—the hypocrites reverse both duties.
rows.anchor: كأنه تعالى يقول الصلاة لي والماعون للخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked why the unbeliever is not named, Rāzī answers that Adam’s lapse was mentioned only after his death and alongside repentance, as a lesson and as evidence of his elevated rank.
rows.anchor: ذكر زلة آدم لكن بعد موته مقرونا بالتوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī closes by contrasting this sūrah about hypocrites with the next sūrah’s description of Muḥammad: the speakers seek pardon for falling short of the Prophet’s obedience without reaching the hypocrites’ evil.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة في ذكر المنافقين والسورة التي بعدها في صفة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After creation for worship and Sūrat al-Kāfirūn’s contrast between Muḥammad’s obedience and the unbelievers’ idolatry, al-Naṣr promises the obedient victory and reward, while al-Masad depicts the disobedient’s worldly loss and punishment hereafter.
rows.anchor: ثم بين في سورة : { قل يا أيها الكافرون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disparity between people’s worldly fortunes is a test of what God gives; the sinner faces swift punishment, while the obedient receives forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: فقال : { ليبلوكم فيما آتاكم }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that after three hidden years, Muḥammad summoned his nearest kin from al-Ṣafā per 26:214, said he could not aid them without monotheism, and Abū Lahab’s curse occasioned the sūrah.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : كان رسول الله يكتم أمره في أول المبعث ويصلي في شعاب مكة ثلاث سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second occasion report says Muḥammad called the Quraysh to al-Ṣafā with “O morning alarm”; after they affirmed they would believe his warning of an approaching enemy, Abū Lahab cursed him and the sūrah was revealed.
rows.anchor: روي أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم صعد الصفا ذات يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third report says Muḥammad gathered his uncles for a meal; they scorned its small appearance, ate their fill while little food vanished, and Abū Lahab rejected the invitation to Islam.
rows.anchor: أنه جمع أعمامه وقدم إليهم طعاما في صحفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a related version Abū Lahab asked what he would gain by becoming Muslim; Muḥammad said what Muslims receive, and Abū Lahab rejected a religion that made him equal to others.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه قال أبو لهب : فمالي إن أسلمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth report says Abū Lahab dissuaded visiting delegations by calling Muḥammad a sorcerer or mad; one delegation insisted on meeting him, and Muḥammad was saddened by the insult before the sūrah descended.
rows.anchor: كان إذا وفد على النبي وفد سألوا عمه عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is destruction: Arabic usage calls an aged, ruined woman “shāba tība,” and the verse about Pharaoh’s plot says it ended in ruin.
rows.anchor: فيه أقاويل ( أحدها ) : التباب الهلاك

rows.speaker: الأعرابي
rows.claim: A Bedouin who had intercourse with his wife during Ramadan said, “I am ruined and have ruined her”; the Prophet did not object, supporting the sense of destruction.
rows.anchor: أن الأعرابي لما واقع أهله في نهار رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If an act belongs to faith or is its weakest part, abandoning it brings ruin; Abū Lahab’s abandonment of belief, speech, and action, together with false belief, speech, and action, certainly merits that meaning.
rows.anchor: ففي حق أبي لهب حصل ترك الاعتقاد والقول والعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is “she lost”: tabāb is loss that ends in destruction, as in the verse saying they increased people only in loss.
rows.anchor: التباب هو الخسران المفضي إلى الهلاك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains tabbat as frustration: Abū Lahab’s trusted status once let him turn visitors away from Muḥammad, but his later hostility made his accusations suspect and defeated his aim.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : لأنه كان يدفع القوم عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of the hand may reflect Abū Lahab’s habit of putting a hand on visitors’ shoulders and pushing them away while calling Muḥammad mad.
rows.anchor: ولعله إنما ذكر اليد لأنه كان يضرب بيده على كتف الوافد عليه

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ explains tabbat as “was defeated”: Abū Lahab thought his hand was uppermost and expected to expel, humiliate, and overpower Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء تبت أي غلبت لأنه كان يعتقد أن يده هي العليا

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb explains the hands as left empty of every good.
rows.anchor: عن ابن وثاب ؛ صفرت يداه على كل خير

rows.speaker: طارق المحاربي
rows.claim: Ṭāriq al-Muḥāribī reports seeing Muḥammad preach in the market while a man behind him stoned him until his heels bled and called him a liar; people identified the man as Abū Lahab.
rows.anchor: روي عن طارق المحاربي أنه قال : رأيت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Hands” can mean the whole person, as in Qurʾānic expressions about what one’s hands have sent ahead or what God’s hands made, and in the proverb “your hands tied it.”
rows.anchor: المراد من اليدين الجملة كقوله تعالى : { ذلك بما قدمت يداك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations take “his hands” as his religion and worldly and future fortunes, or as the means of bringing benefit and warding off harm.
rows.anchor: تبت يداه أي دينه ودنياه أولاه وعقباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that one hand is a weapon and the other a shield.
rows.anchor: أو لأن اليمنى سلاح والأخرى جنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Muḥammad visited Abū Lahab at night to invite him again; after a kid goat miraculously praised the Prophet, Abū Lahab tore its hands and cursed it, which occasioned the verse.
rows.anchor: روي أنه عليه السلام لما دعاه نهارا فأبى

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq reports that Abū Lahab mocked Muḥammad’s promises about the afterlife, blew on his empty hands, and said he saw nothing in them.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحق : يروى أن أبا لهب كان يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes the first clause an imprecation and the second a factual report that it came true, supported by Ibn Masʿūd’s reading “and he was indeed ruined.”
rows.anchor: أنه أخرج الأول مخرج الدعاء عليه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads the second clause as “wa-qad tabb,” “and he was indeed ruined,” supporting the factual reading.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده قراءة ابن مسعود وقد تب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second analysis takes both clauses as reports: the first says Abū Lahab’s deeds perished, the second that he himself perished.
rows.anchor: كل واحد منهما إخبار ولكن أراد بالأول هلاك عمله

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads the first clause as his wealth and the second as Abū Lahab himself, comparing it with people who lose themselves and their families.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth reading makes the first clause Abū Lahab himself and the second his son ʿUtba.
rows.anchor: { تبت يدا أبى لهب } يعني نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says ʿUtba blasphemed to Muḥammad and spat at him; after the Prophet prayed for a beast to attack him, a lion killed him on a journey to Syria.
rows.anchor: اللهم سلط عليه كلبا من كلابك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the sūrah preceded ʿUtba’s death and uses past tense, Rāzī says it reports what God already knew would happen.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان في معلومه تعالى أنه يحصل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth analysis says Abū Lahab’s hands perished because he failed to recognize his Lord’s right, and he himself perished because he failed to recognize the Messenger’s right.
rows.anchor: حيث لم يعرف حق ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with nominative “Abū Lahab” supports treating the kunya as a proper name, answering why he is called Lahab despite having no son by that name.
rows.anchor: أن التكنية قد تكون اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Abū Lahab functions as his name, the kunya need not carry its usual connotation of honor.
rows.anchor: أنه لما كان اسما خرج عن إفادة التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer is that the kunya replaced his birth name, ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.
rows.anchor: أنه كان اسمه عبد العزى فعدل عنه إلى كنيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kunya may suit his fate in a flaming fire, like calling a wicked person “father of evil.”
rows.anchor: أنه لما كان من أهل النار ومآله إلى نار ذات لهب وافقت حاله كنيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “Abū Lahab” may mockingly describe his glowing, flame-colored cheeks and belittle him.
rows.anchor: كنى بذلك لتلهب وجنتيه وإشراقهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Muḥammad was merciful, Abū Lahab obstructed his message by calling him mad; confronting the trusted uncle made his hostility discredit his accusations.
rows.anchor: كان يصرف الناس عن محمد عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muḥammad’s bluntness showed that he would make no religious concession even for an uncle who stood in place of his father.
rows.anchor: أن محمدا لو كان يداهن أحدا في الدين ويسامحه فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinship would normally demand compassion, but Abū Lahab’s extreme hostility merited an equally severe rebuke.
rows.anchor: فلما انقلب الأمر وحصلت العداوة العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not told “say” this because his uncle’s kinship warrants deference; the unbelievers in al-Kāfirūn were not his uncles.
rows.anchor: لأن قرابة العمومة تقتضي رعاية الحرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Kāfirūn the unbelievers attacked God, so God told Muḥammad to answer; here they attacked Muḥammad, so God answers Abū Lahab directly.
rows.anchor: أن الكفار في تلك السورة طعنوا في الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer is that Muḥammad’s silence lets God defend him, consistent with the instruction that the servants of the Merciful answer ignorant people peacefully.
rows.anchor: لما شتموك ، فاسكت حتى تندرج تحت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A report about Abū Bakr says the Prophet explained that while Abū Bakr stayed silent, an angel answered his insulter; when he replied, the angel left and Satan came.
rows.anchor: يروى أن أبا بكر كان يؤذيه واحد فبقي ساكتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī takes the report as a lesson: God defends and aids whoever does not answer a fool directly.
rows.anchor: أن من لا يشافه السفيه كان الله ذابا عنه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير المكي
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr of Mecca reads the hāʾ of “Lahab” without a vowel; Abū ʿAlī says Lahab/Lahab are dialectal variants, like ash-shamʿ and an-nahr.
rows.anchor: قراءة عبد الله بن كثير المكي حيث كان يقرأ : { أبي لهب } ساكنة الهاء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the two forms are dialect variants, but the open hāʾ is preferable because other occurrences have it open.
rows.anchor: يشبه أن يكون لهب ولهب لغتين كالشمع والشمع والنهر والنهر ، وأجمعوا في قوله : { سيصلى نارا ذات لهب } على فتح الهاء

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another scholar says the hāʾ is open in the later occurrence to match the sūrah’s rhyme.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره : إنما اتفقوا على الفتح في الثانية مراعاة لوفاق الفواصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first mā may be an interrogative of denial: what effect could Abū Lahab’s wealth and earnings have in averting punishment? Even Qarūn’s wealth and Sulaymān’s kingdom could not avert death.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون استفهاما بمعنى الإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, mā is a negation: the verse states that wealth and earnings did not benefit him.
rows.anchor: يكون ذلك إخبارا بأن المال والكسب لا ينفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mā in “what he earned” is nominative and may be a relative pronoun (“what he earned”) or a verbal noun (“his earning”).
rows.anchor: ما كسب ) مرفوع وما موصولة أو مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abū Lahab claimed he would ransom himself with his wealth and children if his nephew’s message were true, so this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: إن كان ما يقول ابن أخي حقا فأنا أفتدي منه نفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation takes his wealth and earnings as principal capital and its profits.
rows.anchor: لم ينفعه ماله وما كسب بماله يعني رأس المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another takes the wealth as livestock and what he earned from their offspring and produce.
rows.anchor: أن المال هو الماشية وما كسب من نسلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third distinguishes the wealth inherited from his father from what he acquired himself.
rows.anchor: { ماله } الذي ورثه من أبيه والذي كسبه بنفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says “what he earned” means his children, citing Prophetic sayings that a man’s child is his earning and that a person and his wealth belong to his father.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : { ما كسب } ولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A supporting report says Abū Lahab’s sons fought; when he intervened, one pushed him down, and he angrily called them “the foul earnings.”
rows.anchor: وروي أن بني أبي لهب احتكموا إليه فاقتتلوا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk takes it to mean his wealth and evil deeds, including his plotting against the Messenger.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك : ما ينفعه ماله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says “what he earned” means deeds he thought would benefit him, like deeds rendered as scattered dust.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : { وما كسب } أي عمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense “did not avail” is more emphatic than the future tense in Sūrat al-Layl, as in other Qurʾānic past-tense expressions.
rows.anchor: التعبير بلفظ الماضي يكون آكد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the wealth and earnings failed to help him in opposing the Messenger.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم في عداوة الرسول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others say wealth and earnings failed to save him from the Fire, as the next verse states.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : بل لم يغنيا عنه في دفع النار
